title: Null Pointer Dereference During Pointer Access
symptoms: Segmentation fault (core dumped) or immediate crash when attempting to read or write through a pointer.
roast: You tried to mine diamonds with an empty hand and wondered why your world crashed.
diagnosis: Attempting to dereference a pointer holding NULL (0x0) triggers an operating system memory protection violation because page 0 is unmapped.
debuggingSteps: Check pointer initialization before access
Inspect malloc return value for NULL allocation failures
Add assertion or conditional guard before dereferencing
whyItWorks: Guarding the dereference with a null check and pointing to a valid allocated stack address avoids illegal page faults.

title: Buffer Overflow via Unbounded String Copy (strcpy)
symptoms: Stack smashing detected, corrupted adjacent local variables, or erratic crash on function return.
roast: Shoving an Ender Dragon into a 1x1 dirt hut: your stack didn't stand a chance.
diagnosis: strcpy does not accept a destination buffer size constraint, copying until it finds a null terminator regardless of target boundary.
debuggingSteps: Identify all unbounded string functions (strcpy, strcat, sprintf)
Calculate exact destination buffer capacity including the null terminator
Replace with bounded functions such as snprintf or strncpy with manual null-termination
whyItWorks: snprintf respects sizeof(dest) and guarantees null-termination without spilling over the destination buffer boundary.

sources.title: CERT C Secure Coding Standard - STR31-C

title: Returning Pointer to Local Stack Variable
symptoms: Pointer returns garbage values, or changes unexpectedly when other functions are invoked.
roast: You offered a treasure chest coordinates that despawned the second you walked away.
diagnosis: Stack frames are deallocated upon function return. Returning an address of a local variable produces a dangling pointer referencing invalid stack memory.
debuggingSteps: Inspect function return types returning raw pointers
Verify whether the address belongs to a local automatic storage duration variable
Switch to caller-provided buffer, heap allocation (malloc), or static lifetime
whyItWorks: Heap-allocated memory with malloc persists across function return boundaries until explicitly deallocated with free.

title: Heap Memory Leak from Missing free Call
symptoms: Process RSS memory grows continuously until the operating system kills it with OOM (Out Of Memory).
roast: Spawning creepers endlessly without despawning them: congratulations, your memory just exploded.
diagnosis: Dynamic memory allocated via malloc remains assigned to the process heap until explicitly released via free. Dropping the pointer creates unreachable allocated chunks.
debuggingSteps: Run the program with Valgrind (valgrind --leak-check=full) or AddressSanitizer (-fsanitize=address)
Audit every malloc/calloc call site for corresponding free
Ensure early error returns do not bypass free cleanup
whyItWorks: Invoking free(buf) returns the heap block to the memory manager before function exit.
tests: void *p = malloc(64); assert(p != NULL); free(p); p = NULL;

title: Double Free Memory Corruption
symptoms: Aborted with 'double free or corruption (!prev)' glibc runtime error.
roast: Trying to eat a steak twice in Minecraft: the server just disconnected you for cheating physics.
diagnosis: Passing an already freed pointer to free corrupts the heap metadata binning structures and invites security exploitation or immediate SIGABRT.
debuggingSteps: Trace the ownership lifecycle of the allocated pointer
Assign pointer to NULL immediately following free()
Verify multiple cleanup handlers or conditional branches do not re-free
whyItWorks: Setting p = NULL guarantees subsequent free calls are safe no-ops according to the ANSI C standard.
tests: int *p = malloc(4); free(p); p = NULL; free(p); assert(p == NULL);

title: Reading Uninitialized Local Variable
symptoms: Calculations produce random unpredictable numbers or erratic conditional branching.
roast: Opening an ungenerated loot chest and being shocked it contains random junk stack traces.
diagnosis: Automatic local variables in C contain arbitrary leftover stack garbage until explicitly initialized.
debuggingSteps: Compile with -Wall -Wextra to catch uninitialized variable warnings
Always initialize variables at the point of declaration
Verify conditional initialization covers every branch
whyItWorks: Explicitly zeroing the counter provides a deterministic arithmetic base value.

title: Missing Null Terminator in Character Array
symptoms: strlen and printf('%s') read past array memory into garbage bytes, occasionally segfaulting.
roast: A minecart track with no terminal bumper: you just plummeted straight into the void.
diagnosis: C string routines rely strictly on a sentinel '\0' (ASCII 0) byte to detect end of string. Omitting it causes out-of-bounds reads.
debuggingSteps: Ensure char array size is at least strlen + 1
Explicitly write '\0' at the final position when manually filling arrays
Avoid strncpy without explicit terminal terminator assignment
whyItWorks: Allocating index 3 for '\0' establishes the terminating sentinel required by string formatting functions.

title: Printf Format Specifier Type Mismatch
symptoms: Compiler warning '-Wformat', corrupted numeric output, or segmentation fault when printing strings.
roast: Placing a brewing stand recipe in a furnace: the game doesn't know what you're trying to cook.
diagnosis: Variadic functions like printf rely on format specifiers to determine how many bytes to pop from the argument registers/stack. Mismatched specifiers corrupt stack alignment.
debuggingSteps: Enable -Wformat compiler warning flag
Pair %d with int, %ld with long, %f with double, and %s with char*
Use inttypes.h macros (e.g. PRId64) for fixed-width integer types
whyItWorks: %ld instructs the formatting engine to read the full width of a long integer.

title: Off-By-One Array Out-of-Bounds Loop Indexing
symptoms: Loop overshoots array boundary by 1, corrupting adjacent stack variables.
roast: Walking off the edge of the world block: Minecraft bedrock ends at index N-1, friend.
diagnosis: C arrays are 0-indexed with valid elements [0, N-1]. A loop condition 'i <= N' accesses the invalid index N, causing undefined behavior.
debuggingSteps: Inspect loop condition bounds: verify 'i < N' instead of 'i <= N'
Enable AddressSanitizer (-fsanitize=address) during debug builds
Check sizeof(arr)/sizeof(arr[0]) calculation
whyItWorks: Constraining the loop predicate to 'i < 5' restricts iteration strictly to valid indices 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.
tests: int arr[5]; for(int i = 0; i < 5; i++) arr[i] = i; assert(arr[4] == 4);

title: Misunderstanding Pointer Arithmetic Step Size
symptoms: Pointer advances by unexpected byte offsets, causing alignment errors or data misinterpretation.
roast: You tried to take 4 blocks per step in Nether portal math and landed inside solid obsidian.
diagnosis: Adding 1 to a pointer of type T advances its memory address by sizeof(T) bytes, not 1 byte. Treating byte offsets as element counts causes multi-byte leaps.
debuggingSteps: Remember that (ptr + k) increments memory by k * sizeof(*ptr)
Cast to char* or uint8_t* only if raw single-byte stride is intentional
Avoid mixing byte indexing with typed pointer offsets
whyItWorks: p + 1 advances by 1 element (sizeof(int) bytes), landing cleanly on arr[1].
